ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: The two genes Y and Z of Escherichia coli are adjacent to each other and share one promoter (P) during transcription. A research group isolated a deletion mutant that cannot synthesize Y and Z proteins, but this mutant can synthesize another protein. The 30 amino acid sequence at the amino terminus of this protein is consistent with the sequence at the amino terminus of the Z protein, while the 25 amino acid sequence at the carboxyl terminus is consistent with the sequence at the carboxyl terminus of the Y protein. Based on this, the research group drew the arrangement order diagram of the Y and Z genes in the wild-type strain as shown in the figure. According to this figure, infer the number of DNA bases deleted in the mutant (answer whether the number of deleted bases is an integral multiple of 3, an integral multiple of 3 + 1, or an integral multiple of 3 + 2).
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The number of deleted bases is an integral multiple of 3

The 30 amino acid sequence at the amino terminus of this protein is consistent with the sequence at the amino terminus of the Z protein, while the 25 amino acid sequence at the carboxyl terminus is consistent with the sequence at the carboxyl terminus of the Y protein. Based on this, the research group drew the arrangement order diagram of the Y and Z genes in the wild-type strain as shown in the figure. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The number of deleted bases is an integral multiple of 3
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows that the wild-type DNA is a double-stranded linear structure: the left end of the upper strand is labeled 5′ and the right end is labeled 3′, and the left end of the lower strand is labeled 3′ and the right end is labeled 5′. From left to right, promoter P, the Z gene, an interval/linking region, and the Y gene can be seen in sequence, indicating that in the direction shown in the diagram, after P comes Z first, then Y. In the question stem, the mutant cannot synthesize normal Y protein and Z protein, but can synthesize a fusion protein: its amino-terminal 30 amino acids are consistent with the amino terminus of the Z protein, and its carboxyl-terminal 25 amino acids are consistent with the carboxyl terminus of the Y protein. Therefore, the deletion should directly connect the front segment of the Z gene with the back segment of the Y gene, forming a Z-Y fusion protein. If, after connection, an amino acid sequence consistent with the carboxyl terminus of the Y protein can still be translated, then the reading frame of the Y gene after the connection point must remain unchanged. The genetic code uses 3 bases as one codon. Only when the number of deleted bases is an integral multiple of 3 will the downstream reading frame not undergo a frameshift; if it is 3n+1 or 3n+2, it will cause a frameshift, and the carboxyl-terminal sequence of the Y protein cannot remain consistent. Therefore, the number of DNA bases deleted in the mutant is an integral multiple of 3.
